preamble: Raising and centralization of /a/ to [ɐ] combined with nasalization, giving the nasal vowel [ɐ̃]. Barbosa & Albano (2004), who analyse Brazilian Portuguese nasal vowels as a vowel plus a nasal archiphoneme /N/, give stressed /a/ the nasalized allophone [ɐ̃] both before /N/, as in canta /kaNta/ [kɐ̃ⁿtɐ] '(s/he) sings', and before a nasal consonant in the next syllable, as in sama [sɐ̃mɐ]; oral stressed /a/ stays [a] (saco [sakʊ] 'bag'). Before a heterosyllabic /m n ɲ/ the vowel is raised to [ɐ] even by speakers who do not nasalize it, so Brazilian dama 'lady' is [ˈdɐ̃mɐ] against European [ˈdɐmɐ]. Descriptions that set up nasal vowel phonemes, such as Cruz-Ferreira (1995) for European Portuguese, write /ɐ̃/ directly. The older nasal vowel [ã] that arose from Latin a before n (Old Galician-Portuguese lãa 'wool') is listed under a → ã.

examples.from: canta /kaNta/ '(s/he) sings', stressed /a/ before the nasal archiphoneme
sama 'pine tree leaf', stressed /a/ before heterosyllabic /m/
examples.note: Barbosa & Albano (2004) list it beside cima [sĩmɐ], sema [sẽmɐ] and soma [sõmɐ], the other nasalized allophones in this position.
European Portuguese has [ˈdɐmɐ], raised but oral.

languageExamples.context: Stressed syllables before a nasal: coda /N/ or a nasal consonant beginning the next syllable
